units: a resin applied to the hair increases its grip
the hair drags and then releases the string over and over
this repetition produces a steady oscillation
the speed of the oscillation sets the note that is heard
a string on its own moves too little air
the vibration travels through a piece standing on the body
the body of the instrument begins to move in turn
widening the vibrating surface makes the sound louder
text: Draw a bow across a tight string and the sound starts with a grab so small that the ear never notices it happening. Rosin rubbed into the hair leaves it faintly sticky. So the hair takes hold of the string, drags it a whisker's distance sideways, then lets go. The string springs back, the hair seizes it again, and the cycle repeats without a break. That steady catch and release sets up an even vibration, and how fast it repeats is what fixes the pitch you hear. A string on its own pushes far too little air to carry across a room. It hands its motion instead to the bridge, a thin slip of wood standing upright on the belly. The bridge rocks that broad panel, which in turn shoves a much larger body of air. The sound swells because the surface doing the vibrating has been made wide.

units: the head of the percussion instrument sounded dull at the end of the session
the music director halts the session and sends for the repairer
the dry air had shrunk the animal skin
tightening the fixings would have made things worse
the repairer chooses to add moisture to the room
containers full of water are set around the platform
the group carries on rehearsing in another room
with the suppleness back, a slight adjustment restores the true pitch
text: The rehearsal was nearly over when the timpanist noticed that her drum had stopped answering. Under the stick the head gave back a flat thud, no depth in it, as though every trace of tension had drained away. The conductor stopped the players and sent for the craftsman who looked after the instruments. He found that the very dry air of the hall had shrunk the natural skin, stretched for weeks over the copper bowl. Turning the screws down would only have deepened the imbalance, and it might have split the skin outright. He suggested something gentler: damp the room little by little and let the head slacken on its own. Wide basins of water were set around the platform, and the players moved to another hall to finish. By morning the skin had its give back, and two turns of a key brought the pitch home.

units: you should examine two blades before fitting one
the soft blade bends under the pressure of a finger
the stiff blade keeps its shape when you press it
the blades must be wetted before they are fitted
the fastening must not be tightened too far
you test a low note and then the same note high up
the soft blade answers quickly but weakens in the upper register
the stiff blade asks for more effort and carries loud playing
the choice rests on how tired you feel after a long held sound
text: Lay two reeds side by side and look them over before you fit either one to the mouthpiece. The softer one gives under your thumb; the harder one keeps its curve and pushes back. Each of them suits a different job, so trust the trial rather than the reputation. Wet both blades in a little warm water, then set the first on the table of the mouthpiece and tighten the ligature only just enough to hold it. Blow a long note down low, then the same note up high. The soft blade speaks quickly and the tone comes out sweet, but the high note slips away as soon as you press harder. The hard blade needs more support to start, gives a thicker sound, and holds together when you play loud. Keep whichever tires you least after a long held tone, not the one that charms your ear on the first breath.

units: the place where the instruments are made has taken visitors only lately
a smell of glue and cut wood meets you at the door
the space is divided into four working areas
the first area is where boards are split and joined
a student shapes a piece there by hand with no powered tool
the finishing area is sheltered from moving air
each coat of finish dries before the next one goes on
the last area lets the instrument be tried by playing it
the manager promises that nothing leaves without being tested
the same wood yields instruments that sound different
text: Warm glue and fresh-cut wood hit you the moment you step through the door of the workshop, which opened to visitors only lately. Four stations share the floor. At the back sits the cutting bench, where maple boards are split, folded open, and glued up into the backs of the instruments. On the right comes assembly, and there a young trainee shapes a bridge with a knife, no machine anywhere near her. Further along is the varnish room, kept clear of any draft, where each coat has to dry before the next goes on. The last station, the busiest one, is for trying things out: strings go on, a bow goes across, everyone listens. The manager warns visitors that no piece leaves the shop until it has been played. Most of them go away having learned something odd: two instruments cut from one board never sound alike.

units: the space stands empty late in the day before the session
the technical crew lays the cable and hangs two pickups
the players settle in and tune their instruments
the first take begins once night has fallen
one player fits an accessory that softens the tone
the sound engineer moves a pickup back in response
stray noises can be heard during the pauses
the last take is the best one despite the exhaustion
the gear is packed away before the sun comes up
text: Late in the afternoon the hall stands completely empty, and the quiet inside it feels thick. The technicians come in first, running their cable along the walls and hanging a pair of microphones above the platform. The players drift in afterward in small groups, settle themselves without hurry, and tune their instruments in a calm sort of disorder. The first take starts once night has fallen. A cellist fits a mute onto his bridge to soften the tone, and the engineer at once pulls one microphone back. Between takes you hear paper rustling, a cough, a chair grinding on the floor. Near midnight the tiredness shows on every face, and yet the last take is the one that holds together. The cable is coiled again before dawn, and the hall goes back to its silence, a little warmer than it was.

units: the absence of noise is now sold as a product
the hum of machines makes the ear sort things out very early
this protection of the hearing costs us fineness of listening
attention goes to masses of sound rather than to detail
sound recordings are made to survive the noise around them
those recordings in turn deepen the listener's inattention
the writer describes a loop that feeds itself
bringing back the absence of noise is no longing for the past
text: Quiet has turned into something you buy, and that transformation is worth a moment of thought. Because machines hum everywhere, the ear learns early to filter, to push the drone into the background, to expect nothing from what it takes in. That defense carries a cost of its own. Guarding itself, our listening loses its fineness: it picks out fewer shades and settles for broad blocks of sound. Music follows along, built to survive the noise, squeezed flat, evened out, shaped for half an ear in a corridor. And since that music is what surrounds us, it trains the ear toward still less attention, so the loop closes on itself. Giving silence its place back is no longing for an older time. It is what has to happen if sound is to become an event again rather than scenery nobody notices.

units: the specialist opens the instrument before doing anything else
the middle register gives a sound that is too harsh
she checks the tuning by working on the fastenings of the strings
the trouble stays once that check is done
the padding of the striking parts has packed down with use
grooves have been worn by the contact of the strings
she refuses to replace the parts and would rather restore them
she pierces the padding with points to give it back its spring
she then adjusts the control worked by the left foot
text: Before she touches the keys, the tuner takes off the front panel and studies the inside without a word. The instrument handed to her sounds hard through the middle, as though every note there were struck too bluntly. She checks the tuning first, string by string, with a lever that turns each pin an eighth of a turn. The fault stays. So she looks at the hammers and finds the cause: the felt, packed down by years of playing, has gone hard and carries grooves worn into it by the strings. Her answer is not to swap the parts out but to nurse them. She pricks the felt of every hammer with fine needles to give it back its spring, then sands the surface smooth. Last she sets the left pedal, which brings the hammers closer to the strings, and plays the middle again: the roundness is back.

units: two recordings of the same string work are set against each other
the older recording was made in a space of large dimensions
the echoes there overlap and soften the beginnings of notes
the listener feels placed far away
the other recording was made with pickups very close in
each group of instruments becomes possible to pick out
this precision costs the feeling of space
neither version is declared better than the other
the distant recording suits the calm passages
the close recording suits the fast passages
text: Setting two recordings of one string orchestra score against each other tells you more than an argument about taste ever will. The older one of them, captured in a wide hall, lets the echoes blend as they please; attacks come out rounded, edges a little blurred, and you seem to be listening from the far end of a long room. The other, made with microphones set close in, lays out every section: you can catch the scrape of the bows, the breathing of the players, the grain of the lower strings. That sharpness costs something, since the whole loses the depth that gave the earlier version its breadth. Neither one of them wins outright. The distant recording persuades in the slow movements, the close one takes over in the fast passages, where the clarity of the line decides everything.

units: the writer answers a request for news of his learning
the first sessions went on holding the instrument without making a sound
that early constraint spared his shoulders
the teacher asks for a breath that comes from the belly
an uneven stream of air makes the note waver
the nimbleness of the fingers comes along by itself once the basics hold
hearing is the faculty that takes longest to form
the writer now catches his own tuning mistakes before they are pointed out
he invites the reader to come and listen the following week
text: You asked me how the lessons were going, so here is what a whole season of them has taught me. Posture came first: I spent the early sessions just holding the instrument without playing a single note, which felt completely ridiculous at the time and which saved my shoulders. Then breathing. My teacher insists the air start from the belly and reach the mouthpiece steadily, or else the note wobbles and fades out into nothing. Fingers come third, and they sort themselves out on their own as soon as the other two points hold up. The ear ripens slowest of all: I am starting to hear that I am out of tune before anyone tells me, and that turns out to be more encouraging than it sounds. Come round next week, bring your own instrument along if you like, and judge the result for yourself.

units: she started out with cleaning and tidying jobs
she had no access to the mixing gear during her first year
she was then given the placing of pickups on the drums
an accessory badly fitted on a brass instrument can spoil a take
the hardest thing was keeping her remarks to herself
she ran a session alone to cover for a missing colleague
that successful session put an end to the menial jobs
she now teaches the trade to newcomers
her main advice is to trust the ear and not the eye
text: The first question put to her is where she began. She swept the studio, she says, coiled cable and carried crates of equipment around, and never laid a hand on the desk for an entire year. And after that? After that they let her set microphones on the drums, then on the brass, where a single badly placed mute can ruin an entire take. And the hardest part of those early days? Keeping quiet whenever she could hear a fault that the others were letting slide. In the end she ran the desk on her own one night, standing in for a colleague who had fallen ill; the session went perfectly well, and nobody ever handed her a broom again. And now? Now she trains up beginners, and she keeps repeating the one rule she believes in: you place a microphone with your ears, never with your eyes.
